title: Salt and light
hook: ye are the salt of the earth, the light of the world (Matthew 5:13–16)
tomorrow: what if you remember a fight halfway through a prayer?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Psalms closed on every thing that hath breath, and a hallelujah. Today the reading moves to Matthew: a sermon, preached on a hill.
screen: `EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.` → `A SERMON ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: Somebody did a good thing on Saturday: picked up trash on a trail, served at a shelter, sat with a neighbor. Now there's a photo, and a question. Post it, or not? Half of it feels like bragging; half of it might get someone else out there. That's yesterday's question, Zoe's question, and an old one. Matthew says Jesus saw the crowds, went up into a mountain, sat down, and began to teach. A few lines in, he walks straight into it.
screen: `A GOOD THING, AND A PHOTO.` → `BRAGGING, OR AN INVITATION?` → `UP INTO A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Right after the blessings that open the sermon, Jesus tells his listeners who they are. "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?" Salt does its work by disappearing into the food. You taste the meal, not the salt. Then the opposite picture: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Nobody lights a lamp, he says, and puts it under a bushel, a basket; it goes on a stand to light the whole house. Then the line: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Look where the credit goes. The good works are seen, but the praise isn't meant to land on the one who did them. It passes through. That's the teaching: Christians read salt and light as a calling for ordinary followers, not a few heroes, to be useful and visible in the world in a way that points past themselves to God. One to tell a friend: he says ye are, not ye should be. He tells them what they already are. And hold this one: a few lines later, the same sermon says do your giving in secret. Both are in the same sermon, and you'll hear how they fit.
screen: `YE ARE THE SALT OF THE EARTH.` · `A CITY ON A HILL CANNOT BE HID.` · `SEEN, SO THE PRAISE GOES PAST YOU.` · `YE ARE, NOT YE SHOULD BE.` · then, large: `SALT AND LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Choose one small good thing to do in the open this week: holding a door, thanking someone by name in front of others, picking up litter where people walk. Plan the place and the time in one sentence. Then sit, and let it be ordinary.
Salt and light: Jesus's two pictures of his listeners, one that disappears into the meal and one that can't be hid.
The line to keep: salt and light, seen so the praise goes past you. The sermon has started; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read the salt and light sayings (Matthew 5:13–16) as a calling to visible good works that point to God; the passage is read in churches and often taught at confirmations and commissioning services.

fork.setup: your book club raised money for a family whose house burned, and the local paper wants a story. what does salt and light suggest?
options: do the story, and keep the focus on the family's need and the help, not the club.
turn it down; a good deed loses its worth the moment anyone sees it.
do it, and make sure every member's name is printed so each one is thanked.
fork.reveal: light is meant to be seen, so others see the good and give glory past you. the spotlight goes on the work, not the workers.

chat.says: my temp boss wants my trail-cleanup photo on the company page. feels like bragging. post it?
options: Post it, but point it past yourself, at the trail and the work. Light is for others to see by.
Don't post. Real goodness always stays hidden; once it's seen online, it doesn't count.
Post it with your name big. The sermon says let people see your good works, so own it.
chat.meaning: Jesus says let your light shine so people see the good works and glorify the Father, not the doer. Seen, but pointing past yourself.
